# THEORYs with `tags` `ecology`

*Topics — What a work is about. Nucleation holds whatever reading the owner files here, whether or not an Anthology of the SOTA topic could also hold it; instruction for ML practice belongs to the anthology (ADR-048). The words are seeded from the clusters the reading-time triage of 2026-09-25 found, and grow by decision.*

**Ecology** — how organisms interact with each other and their environment — symbiosis and host–microbe partnerships, competition, herbivory and trophic interactions, community structure, resilience and regime shifts in ecosystems (ADR-028). How a partner comes to live inside another and depend on it is endosymbiosis (ADR-055).

| [THEORY-128](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-128.md) | After mass bleaching, coral recovery on a reef crest depends on large herbivorous fishes keeping macroalgae down, because recovery runs through recruitment and survival that macroalgae suppress, not through the persistence of surviving colonies alone | Hughes et al. (2007), [LIT-711](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-711.md). On the reef crest at Orpheus Island after the 1998 bleaching, four roofless cages kept large and medium fishes out of 25 m² plots for 30 months. Macroalgae averaged 56% cover inside against 4.1% and 1.7% in controls. Coral cover reached 7.7% inside against 19.2% and 20.2%, with recruitment about two-thirds lower and mortality of established colonies more than double. Control recovery came mainly from recruits of taxa bleaching had removed. Proposed: one site, four replicates, plot scale, and fish exclusion standing in for herbivore exclusion. The algal state vanished within 30 days of reopening. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-130](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-130.md) | Coral bleaching is the breakdown of a regulated host–symbiont exchange, reached by more than one route, not a single mechanism of symbiont loss | Two reviews, with no data of their own. Boilard et al. (2020), [LIT-712](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-712.md), collect the regulators of the coral–dinoflagellate exchange: the host controls symbiont density, bacteria shift the nitrogen supply, and heat leads either to host rejection of symbionts (apoptosis, autophagy, exocytosis, detachment, necrosis) or to pigment loss under oxidative stress. Goulet et al. (2020), [LIT-709](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-709.md), report two octocorals whose similar symbiont losses at +3 °C came by different routes, one by fewer symbionts per host cell and one by loss of host cells. Proposed. The claim that the wider microbiome drives bleaching is declined: its own source says it cannot yet be tested. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-132](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-132.md) | Stability, a system's speed of return to equilibrium after disturbance, and resilience, its capacity to absorb change and persist within its domain of attraction, are distinct properties that can trade off, so a system can be highly unstable and highly resilient, and managing it for constancy can erode its resilience | Holling (1973), [LIT-741](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-741.md). Stability is return to equilibrium. Resilience is persistence under change, set by the extent of the domain of attraction and the system's distance from its edge. Budworm forests and insect populations in harsh climates are unstable and resilient; homogeneous lakes are stable and fragile. Active for the distinction, which has become standard. The claim that management for constancy erodes resilience rests on suggestive cases. | Active |
| [THEORY-136](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-136.md) v6 | A persistent or abrupt change is not evidence that a system has alternative stable states: field patterns such as jumps, multimodality and dual relationships also arise from a stepwise driver or a simple threshold, and only hysteresis, initial-state dependence or a lasting shift after a temporary disturbance, with slow return excluded, comes close to showing one | Scheffer & Carpenter (2003), [LIT-726](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-726.md). Alternative attractors predict sudden shifts, multimodal states and dual responses to a driver, and so do discontinuous drivers and threshold responses. Discriminating evidence is experimental: different starting states reaching different end states, temporary disturbances causing lasting shifts, or hysteresis. Slow recovery can mimic all three. Positive feedback must be strong to produce alternative states. Active as a methodological standard. | Active |
| [THEORY-469](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-469.md) | Because persistence (mean absolute fitness at least 1) and selection (fitness differences) are logically independent, niche construction theory's evolutionary niche, read externally as the factors producing fitness differences in a population, differs in extension from the realized population ecological niche even after unit and modality are matched, so it is not a simple translation of Hutchinson's niche | Trappes (2021), [LIT-169](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-169.md), read in [NOTE-155](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-155.md). The non-identity follows from a conceptual argument the reading grades strong. The three kinds of case that populate the gap are weaker: habitat degradation rests on a projected persistence failure, commensalism on one field study after the author's first candidate failed, and non-limiting resources on a "possible example". The result is scoped to Odling-Smee, Laland & Feldman's 2003 niche concept and to the externalist reading of selection pressure. It does not say the two niches differ much; they "still coincide to a large extent". | Active |
| [THEORY-473](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-473.md) | Scaled down to one organism, Hutchinson's niche, defined as the conditions that give that individual an expected lifetime reproductive success of at least one, is observed only as a point; the rest of it is counterfactual, reached by translocation in only a few dimensions and otherwise inferred from other individuals, so in practice it is the niche of a phenotype class, and its authors call it mostly metaphorical | Takola & Schielzeth (2022), [LIT-127](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-127.md), read in full in [NOTE-170](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-170.md). The working definition (p. 5) gives the individualized niche an absolute-fitness boundary, expected LRS ≥ 1, and splits it into realized, potential, time-slice, prospective and trajectory-based niches. That the realized niche is a point and the potential niche unobservable follows from the definitions. The paper concedes there is "no empirical solution" at the individual level (p. 15), and its fix, marginalizing fitness functions across individuals, is schematic. It is a framework for structuring research, by its authors' own account, not a measurement. | Active |
| [THEORY-548](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-548.md) v4 | In generalised Lotka–Volterra dynamics with every interaction delayed by τ, a feasible equilibrium that is stable without delay loses stability at τ_c = min over the community eigenvalues j of arctan(\|Re j\|/\|Im j\|)/\|j\|, where a pair of roots crosses the imaginary axis transversally (a Hopf point), so the critical delay is set by the community spectrum; in Saeedian et al.'s strongly self-regulated setting the oscillating regime's community-level variability falls with diversity (S = 10–70) while species-level variability rises, and the fall matches what summing independently oscillating species gives | Saeedian et al. (2021), [LIT-057](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-057.md), a preprint, read in [NOTE-061](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-061.md). The critical delay is the linear delay result on the community matrix, re-derived on promotion (2026-10-20), and matched simulation at one strongly self-regulated setting. The variability result was re-run on promotion against an averaging null and matches it: the fall of community-level variability with diversity is what summing independent oscillators gives, not an ecological stabilisation. | Active |
| [THEORY-560](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-560.md) | In rodents, gut microbes can drive stress and affect-related behaviour through vagal, immune, endocrine and metabolite routes, and faecal transplant from depressed people partly transfers the phenotype; in people, probiotics have so far shown at most small reductions in subjective stress in healthy volunteers, and strains with strong preclinical records have failed in controlled trials | Forssten et al. (2022), [LIT-915](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-915.md), read in [NOTE-703](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-703.md). A narrative review with no search method, by employees of a probiotics manufacturer, which documents its own translational failures: L. rhamnosus JB-1 had no effect on any outcome against placebo after "comprehensive preclinical evidence". The rodent half is well documented; the human half rests on one meta-analysis of healthy volunteers and trials with nulls. Proposed because the source is a narrative industry review; the gap it describes runs against its authors' interest. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1048](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1048.md) v2 | On the Black Queen Hypothesis of Morris, Lenski and Zinser, losing a costly function whose product leaks to neighbours is favoured by ordinary individual selection in large free-living microbial populations, and the loss proceeds until the remaining producers just supply the community, so that most cells come to depend on a rare few with no relatedness, cooperation or collective required | Morris, Lenski & Zinser (2012), [LIT-1568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1568.md), read in [NOTE-1212](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1212.md). A loss-of-function mutant invades when its resource saving B = (Q_A − Q_M)/Q_A exceeds its cost C, which falls as other cells' leaky activity protects it. Because protection falls as producers become rare, the loss is frequency dependent and stops short of community-wide loss. The evidence is Prochlorococcus's loss of katG and its dependence on a peroxide-removing community. The dependence it produces is one-way, from beneficiaries to helpers, and involves no collective. | Active |
| [THEORY-1162](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1162.md) v3 | In a consumer-resource model whose species-resource benefits and impacts have correlation rho, the replica-symmetric cavity fixed point loses stability where rho squared equals surviving species over non-depleted resources | Blumenthal, Rocks and Mehta (2024), [LIT-1236](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1236.md): in MacArthur's consumer–resource model with benefits c and impacts e correlated by ρ, the replica-symmetric steady state is unstable when ρ < ρ*, ρ*² = S*/M* at the boundary. With ρ = 1 competitive exclusion keeps S*/M* ≤ 1, so the symmetric model never crosses it. What this does not say: that non-reciprocity by itself breaks the optimization picture; it does so only past a boundary set by species packing, and that the other side is chaotic is shown numerically, not derived. | Active |
| [THEORY-1168](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1168.md) v2 | In a Lotka–Volterra community with a symmetric interaction matrix, the growth-weighted biomass rᵀx strictly increases along every edge of the invasion graph, so the invasion graph has no cycles | Re-derived from Serván and Allesina (2021), [LIT-1824](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1824.md), read in [NOTE-1422](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1422.md), and applied to Hofbauer and Schreiber's invasion graph ([LIT-1233](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1233.md)). At an equilibrium V = 2rᵀx − xᵀAx equals rᵀx, and for two equilibria the difference is a sum of invasion growth rates weighted by abundances, which an edge of the invasion graph makes positive. [THEORY-1510](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1510.md)'s old condition asked only for a second reader of the paper, so this entry's condition is new, drafted at that review: the authors concede that rigorous tests of alternative stable states are beyond most restoration efforts, and [THEORY-136](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-136.md)'s bar applies. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1659](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1659.md) | Fanning and Raworth (2025) find that, measured as 35 indicators each against its own social or planetary threshold, global social shortfall fell modestly between 2000 and 2022 while ecological overshoot grew, and that disaggregating by income cluster shows the richest fifth of countries contributing over 40% of overshoot and the poorest 40% bearing over 60% of shortfall, an inequality the global aggregates mask. | Fanning & Raworth (2025), read in [NOTE-1782](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1782.md) (Read). A third iteration of the Doughnut: 21 dimensions measured by 35 indicators (social foundation and ecological ceiling), with time series 2000–2022 for 30 of them, plus a 2017 disaggregation of 27 comparable indicators into three country clusters by income (poorest 40%, middle 40%, richest 20% of countries). Globally, deprivation fell modestly while ecological overshoot rose; disaggregated, the richest cluster contributes a disproportionate share of overshoot and the poorest holds most shortfall. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1667](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1667.md) | Brenninger, Zug and Kokko (2025) give a unified minimal model in which a reproductive manipulator's spread is set by infected females' relative fecundity, vertical transmission and manipulation efficiency, and argue that cytoplasmic incompatibility's positive frequency dependence makes it hard to invade but hard to displace, a priority effect that may explain its prevalence despite poorer invasion prospects. | Brenninger, Zug & Kokko (2025), read in [NOTE-1786](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1786.md) (Skimmed). A unified minimal model of the infection dynamics of maternally transmitted endosymbionts (Wolbachia, Rickettsia, Cardinium, Spiroplasma and others) that manipulate arthropod reproduction: male-killing, feminization, parthenogenesis induction, sex-allocation distortion and cytoplasmic incompatibility (CI), in diplodiploid and haplodiploid hosts. It gives invasion criteria for single strains and for pairs of manipulators. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1684](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1684.md) | Rockström and colleagues (2026) set out the Earth Commission's programme for 2024–2027: to extend quantified "safe" boundaries (protecting Earth-system resilience) and "just" boundaries (minimizing significant harm to people, other species and future generations) to novel entities and the ocean, and to translate them, by transcription into aggregate pressure budgets and then allocation among actors under stated fairness principles, into targets for countries, cities and companies, treating justice as a structural condition of planetary stability. | Rockström, Denton, Norström et al., read in [NOTE-1796](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1796.md) (Read). A commentary setting out the Earth Commission's second phase (2024–2027). It recaps the first phase: "safe" Earth system boundaries (protecting Earth-system resilience) and "just" boundaries (minimizing significant harm to people and ecosystems, by the "3 I" approach: interspecies, intergenerational, intragenerational justice), quantified for climate, biosphere, nutrients (N, P), freshwater and aerosols, globally and sub-globally; and "just access", minimum resource thresholds for a dignified life, forming the floor. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1714](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1714.md) | Cuny and Poelman review evidence that koinobiont parasitoids regulate the development and feeding of the herbivores they grow inside, usually arresting but sometimes prolonging host growth and in some species switching with conditions, through polydnaviruses, venom, teratocytes and larval secretions that act on the host's own hormones, and that these changes in the host alter how plants respond to herbivory. | Cuny and Poelman (2022), Evolution of koinobiont parasitoid host regulation and consequences for indirect plant defence, read in [NOTE-1756](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1756.md) (Skimmed). Koinobiont parasitoids let the host keep feeding while their larvae develop inside it, and regulate the host's growth: usually arresting it (smaller hosts eating less), sometimes prolonging it (larger hosts eating more), and some species switch with conditions. The regulation is done by injected and secreted factors, and it changes the plant's responses to the parasitized herbivore, so it reaches the wider community. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1716](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1716.md) | van Roosmalen and de Bekker (2024) review evidence that Ophiocordyceps changes carpenter-ant behaviour while leaving the ant's nervous tissue intact, plausibly through secreted effectors and by disrupting and resetting the ant's biological clock, and argue from parallels in other summit-inducing parasites that these mechanisms likely evolved convergently, while stating that the evidence so far is correlative. | van Roosmalen & de Bekker (2024), read in [NOTE-1766](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1766.md) (Read). Review of what is proposed about how Ophiocordyceps unilateralis s.l. infects carpenter ants and changes their behaviour (loss of daily rhythm, reduced communication with nestmates, hyperactivity, staggering, summiting, biting at about solar noon, death), compared with other behaviour-manipulating parasites (Entomophthora in flies, baculovirus in caterpillars, and others). Two hypothesised mechanism families: secreted fungal effectors (enterotoxins, an aflatrem-like alkaloid cluster, protein tyrosine phosphatases, juvenile-hormone modulation, small secreted proteins predicted to bind ant GPCRs), and disruption and resetting of the host's biological clock. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1717](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1717.md) | Hafer-Hahmann's phylogenetic meta-analysis of 1,635 observations on trophically transmitted helminths finds that mature parasites consistently make hosts more susceptible to predation while immature stages have little or inconsistent effect, that mature parasites dominate mixed infections, that manipulation is stronger when the correct predator is present, and that phylogeny and the ecological drivers theory proposes explain little of the variation. | Hafer-Hahmann (2026), The Evolution and Ecology of Host Manipulation in Helminth Parasites, read in [NOTE-1730](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1730.md) (Read). A Bayesian phylogenetic meta-analysis (brms) of host manipulation by trophically transmitted helminths: 1,635 observations, 207 papers, 82 parasite and 80 host taxa. Effect size is Cohen's d for infected vs uninfected hosts, signed by assumed effect on predation susceptibility. | Proposed |
